It also features Gustav Klimt's Beethoven Frieze, one of the best-known works in the Secession style, a branch of Art Nouveau. The building appears on the national side of Austria's 50-cent euro coin.

Grundtvig's Church, in Copenhagen's Bispebjerg district, is a rare case of expressionist church architecture. Named for N. F. S. Grundtvig, a Danish pastor, philosopher and writer of hymns, it went to competition, which Peder Vilhelm Jensen-Klint won in 1913. To prepare, Klint studied many Danish village churches, especially the stepped-gable churches of Zealand. He joined the modern geometry of Brick Expressionism to the upward pull of Gothic building. It took some five million yellow bricks, a standard Danish material; the yellow brick and the lack of ornament stress the height while keeping a spare modern look. The west front, which recalls a westwork or the case of a church organ, includes the 49-metre bell tower. After Klint's death in 1930 his son Kaare Klint took over, and work on the interior and nearby buildings went on until 1940.

The Mieczysław Karłowicz Philharmonic of Szczecin, Poland, was founded in 1948, and since 14 September 2014 it has been based in a new building at 48 Małopolska Street by Studio Barozzi Veiga of Barcelona. The 13,000-square-metre venue holds a main concert hall seating 1,000, a smaller hall for 200 and several conference rooms. Its ice-like form and translucent ribbed glass skin, which glows white at night, have made it a new emblem of the city. Krzysztof Penderecki wrote a fanfare for the opening ceremony, played by the Szczecin Philharmonic Orchestra. The building took first prize for Architectural Design of the Year at the Eurobuild Awards 2014, and in 2015 it received the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture.

Above Liberec in the Czech Republic, Ještěd Tower crowns Mount Ještěd as a television transmitter that also contains a hotel and restaurant in its lowest levels. It stands 94 metres tall and is made of reinforced concrete in a hyperboloid form. Karel Hubáček designed it, with Zdeněk Patrman on structural statics and Otakar Binar on the interior furnishings. The team spent three years on the design, from 1963 to 1966, and construction took another seven, to 1973. The hyperboloid was chosen because it carries the line of the hill upward and copes with the harsh climate at the top. In 1969 Hubáček received the Perret Prize of the International Union of Architects. A Czech cultural monument since 1998 and a national cultural monument since 2006, the tower joined UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List in 2007.

The campus of the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore was designed under B. V. Doshi, later the 2018 Pritzker Prize laureate. Design started in 1977 and the buildings were finished in 1983. Its sources were Fatehpur Sikri, the 16th-century city near Agra, Madurai's 13th-century Meenakshi Temple and the gardens of Bangalore. Light and environment were central to the poly-nuclear plan, which blends traditional Indian architecture with the ideas of the Team 10 modernists. The first complex, 54,000 square metres, uses exposed concrete and hand-chipped granite masonry. Tall passages, trellises, sunlit pergolas, semi-open corridors, green quadrangles, geometric roofs and Kota stone floors stand out. When Dezeen asked thirteen leading Indian architecture firms for their favourite building, IIMB was the only one named by more than one, and it was called "the most influential piece of (Indian) modern architecture".

Begun in 1993, the India Habitat Centre in New Delhi is a building with many uses. HUDCO, the public Housing and Urban Development Corporation, needed offices for its staff and took the unusual step of inviting selected non-profit groups working on habitat to share the building. Joseph Allen Stein, its architect, and Santosh Sharma, HUDCO's chairman, turned the brief from an office building into a piece of urban design. Members share services indoors and out: several courtyards, common meeting rooms, parking, a library, restaurants, a museum and hotels, some of them open to the public. Five blocks, linked by aerial walkways, sit on nine acres in the city, and the centre can host up to 20 events at once, from social and cultural events and exhibitions to business events. The building turned away from traditional materials and methods of construction.

The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur is a group of 19 instruments for astronomy, built by Sawai Jai Singh, the Rajput king who founded the city, and completed in 1734. With them, astronomical positions can be observed with the naked eye. The instruments are made of local stone and marble, and each has an astronomical scale, usually marked on its marble lining. The site has the world's largest stone sundial. The Vrihat Samrat Yantra, or "great king of instruments", is 88 feet (27 m) high, one of the largest sundials anywhere, and its face is tilted at 27 degrees, matching Jaipur's latitude. It is on UNESCO's World Heritage List, and UNESCO judges it India's most significant historic observatory and the one in the best condition, a record of what ancient India knew about astronomy and the cosmos.

Sri Lanka's Parliament stands on Duwa, a 5-hectare island in the Diyawanna Oya at Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, the administrative capital, roughly 16 kilometres east of Colombo. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa won Parliament's approval for a new building there on 4 July 1979, and that year President J. R. Jayewardene asked Geoffrey Bawa to design it. The Japanese contractors Mitsui helped deliver the work, which kept to its planned 26 months, and Jayewardene opened the complex on 29 April 1982. Its design is regional modernism: modernist in approach, yet respectful of Sri Lanka's vernacular building tradition. The layout hints at symmetry, which sets it sharply apart from the organic shape of the surrounding lake. In 1983 the Pacific Area Travel Association gave the complex a Heritage Award of Recognition for design in the tradition of local vernacular architecture.

Leila Araghian spent four years designing Tabiat Bridge, a 270-metre crossing that joins Taleghani Park to Abo-Atash Park over Modarres Expressway, a main highway in northern Tehran. Wanting people to stop and reflect rather than simply pass, she made the bridge bend and gave it benches and seating. Three tree-shaped columns carry two continuous decks, leaving the lower one covered and usable in every season; a third level sits where the truss meets the branching columns. The steel truss is three-dimensional, and the curved surface varies in width. Restaurants stand at both ends, kiosks and seating lie between, and openings let trees grow through. Built from 2010 to October 2014 with 2,000 tonnes of steel and 10,000 cubic metres of concrete, it drew four million visitors in its first year and won a 2016 Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Abbas the Great of the Safavid Empire ordered the Shah Mosque, begun in 1611 and finished around 1630. The main foundation inscription, above the door of the entrance iwan, names Ali Akbar Isfahani as architect. Since the square does not line up with the qibla (Mecca's direction), a large vestibule turns roughly 45 degrees to the southwest so the rest of the mosque can face the right way for prayer. The plan follows the four-iwan layout common in Iranian congregational mosques. A dome 52 metres high and about 25 metres wide covers the main prayer hall; it has two shells, after earlier Timurid domes, with 14 metres between them. The tiles use the then-new haft rangi, or seven-colour, style. With Naghsh-e Jahan Square and nearby structures, the mosque is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In January 2004 Preston Scott Cohen won the Herta and Paul Amir design competition for a new wing at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art. The estimated budget of $45 million covered flexible galleries and concessions, along with restoring labs and offices. The wing is known for its hyperboloid form, and Israeli stone was chosen for its finish. Its five floors hold 18,500 square feet of galleries, a new photography and visual arts section, and an Israeli Architecture Archive. Renderings of the design appeared in Skin + Bones, a 2006–2007 exhibition on fashion and architecture at Los Angeles's Museum of Contemporary Art. It opened in November 2011 on the museum's western side.

In 1962 the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer was commissioned to design the International Fair of Tripoli, formally named Rachid Karami International Exhibition Center, as a complex of buildings for a World's Fair planned in the city. Building stopped in 1975 when the Lebanese civil war broke out, and it never restarted. The grounds hold 15 Niemeyer buildings left partly finished, spread over about 75.6 hectares near the southern entrance to Tripoli. In 2023 the fair was inscribed on the World Heritage List and, at the same time, listed as World Heritage in Danger.

Founded in 1948, the University of Ibadan started as University College Ibadan, attached to the University of London, which oversaw its academic programmes and awarded its degrees until 1967. It was set up as the first institution in Nigeria able to award degrees, after the narrow goals of Yaba College and pressure from Nigerian nationalists for fuller education. The first sod for the permanent campus was cut on 17 November 1948, a day the university now calls Founders' Day. Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew, both modernists, designed its first buildings, and The Times regarded Ibadan as the most notable of Fry's works in West Africa. The campus today has 15 halls of residence, which house about 30% of students in the regular mode of study.

Renzo Piano designed The Shard, a 95-storey mixed-use skyscraper in Southwark, London, shaped as a pyramid and once called London Bridge Tower. At 309.6 metres, no building in the UK or Western Europe is taller. Piano saw it as a spire-like sculpture rising from the Thames, inspired by the railway lines beside the site, Canaletto's paintings of London spires and sailing ships' masts. Angled glass panes on its façades are meant to reflect sunlight and sky, so the tower's look shifts with weather and season. English Heritage warned it would pierce historic London like 'a shard of glass', and the name stuck. Construction, begun in March 2009, used top-down methods, a first for the UK. Opened in July 2012, it holds offices, three restaurants, a five-star hotel, ten apartments and the highest viewing gallery in the UK.

Renzo Piano designed the New York Times Building with Fox & Fowle; the 52-storey tower at 620 Eighth Avenue, near Times Square in Midtown Manhattan, was his first design in New York City. The two firms were chosen through an architectural competition, the land was bought in 2003 after disputes with the owners, and the building was finished in 2007 at a cost of more than $1 billion. Its plan is cruciform, with a steel frame and a braced mechanical core. About 186,000 ceramic rods, which the architects called 'baguettes', line the facade to deflect heat and glare, and they shift in colour with sun and weather. Floor-to-ceiling glass brings in daylight and stands for the transparency of the media, while the notched corners leave their steel exposed and unscreened, expressing the ideal of transparency in journalism.

The Spanish architect, engineer and artist Santiago Calatrava designed Turning Torso, a neo-futurist residential tower in Malmö that opened on 27 August 2005. It rises 190 metres over 54 storeys and contains 147 apartments. Its form comes from his white marble sculpture Twisting Torso, based on the form of a twisting person. Nine five-storey pentagonal segments rotate against each other as the tower climbs, leaving the top a quarter turn clockwise of the ground floor. Each floor is an irregular pentagon turning around a vertical core, with an exterior steel framework for support. One aim was to give Malmö a recognisable skyline again after the nearby Kockums Crane was removed in 2002. In 2005 it received the Gold Emporis Skyscraper Award; in 2015 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat gave it a 10 Year Award.

Designed by Jean Nouvel, the Musée du quai Branly in Paris presents indigenous art and cultures from Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas; a jury and international competition to choose its architect began in early 1999. Planned to fit its neighbours, the main building looks lower than those around it, partly hidden by gardens, and bends with the Seine, while three administrative buildings harmonise with the adjoining Haussmann-era blocks. The main block works like a bridge raised 10 metres over the garden on two concrete silos and 26 steel columns. Thirty galleries appear on the north side as coloured boxes. Inside, Nouvel left out walls, barriers and railings to free objects from conventional display. Gilles Clément's gardens reject French formality, a high double glass wall blocks most street noise, and Patrick Blanc's living wall covers 800 m² of façade.

Paolo Portoghesi designed and directed the Great Mosque of Rome with Vittorio Gigliotti and Sami Mousawi. Planning took over ten years: Rome's city council donated the land in 1974, President Sandro Pertini attended the laying of the first stone in 1984, and the inauguration came on 21 June 1995. Covering 30,000 square metres, with room for over 12,000 worshippers, it is the Western world's largest mosque, and it also houses the Italian Islamic Cultural Centre. Over the main prayer hall, a central dome more than 20 metres high is ringed by 16 smaller ones. Palm-shaped columns stand for the link between God and each believer, light and shade are meant to create a meditative mood, and travertine and cotto recall traditional Roman building. The minaret was trimmed slightly so it ends about a metre lower than St Peter's dome.

La Seine Musicale is a centre for music and the performing arts on Île Seguin, an island in the Seine lying between Sèvres and Boulogne-Billancourt, west of Paris. Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines designed its first buildings, which opened in April 2017. The programme includes a raised, egg-shaped theatre in the round, mainly for classical music, and a larger concert hall where pop stars perform. The unamplified Patrick-Devedjian Auditorium seats 1,150, while Grande Seine, a modular hall set lower on the island, holds up to 6,000. A large curved solar array that can move covers the smaller auditorium and supplies much of the daytime energy. Rehearsal studios, seminar rooms, a press centre, restaurants and a big roof garden complete the site. Laurence Equilbey conducted Insula orchestra and the Accentus choir at the opening concert on 22 April 2017.

In Astana, Kazakhstan's capital, the Palace of Peace and Reconciliation is a 62-metre pyramid serving as an event venue and a non-denominational national spiritual centre. It was completed in 2006 to host a congress of world and traditional religious leaders held every three years. The steel-framed pyramid rests on a 15-metre earth-covered block, and concrete forms the lower levels; the building's lower portion, in three 'stories' of triangles, has pale granite cladding. Given the extreme climate, engineers fixed one corner and set the other three on bridge bearings, a bridge-building method never before used in a building. Inside are an opera house with 1,300 seats, a national museum of culture, a library and a research centre. Delegates meet in a round chamber modelled on the UN Security Council room, under stained glass in the flag's gold and pale blue.

The European Central Bank held an international design competition in 1999, won by the Vienna practice Coop Himmelb(l)au. In Frankfurt the bank's site combines a skyscraper of two towers with the Großmarkthalle, once the city's wholesale market, and a low-rise block joining them. Between the towers, an atrium carries four interchange platforms. The taller north tower rises to a roof of 185 metres over 45 storeys; its southern partner reaches 165 metres over 43. The market hall dates from 1926–1928, part of the New Frankfurt programme, and was then the widest monocoque building in the world; it was fully renovated for the bank. The scheme cost 1.3 to 1.4 billion euros, was finished in 2014 and had its official opening on 18 March 2015.

Mecanoo, working with the engineers Buro Happold, was named winner of the design competition for the Library of Birmingham in early August 2008. It stands on Centenary Square in the western part of the city centre, next to Baskerville House and the Birmingham Rep; the library links to the Rep and shares some facilities with it. Opening on 3 September 2013, it replaced Birmingham Central Library. Descriptions have called it the UK's largest public library, Europe's largest public cultural space and Europe's largest regional library. An aquifer ground source system cuts its energy use: cold water pumped from underground feeds the air conditioning. On 17 July 2014 it joined the six-building shortlist for the 2014 Stirling Prize, the award for excellence in architecture.

Moshe Safdie designed Marina Bay Sands, a 20-hectare resort in Singapore, and says card decks first inspired it. The three towers taper from broad bases; each rests on two unequal legs, the curved eastern one leaning on the other, a hard construction challenge. Atop them runs the Sands SkyPark, a 340-metre skyway for 3,902 people with a 150-metre infinity pool. It sits on the world's largest cantilevered public platform, projecting 66.5 metres beyond the north tower. The SkyPark's hull came as 14 prefabricated steel sections joined on top of the towers, and four movement joints under the main pools help them withstand the towers' motion. The resort holds a hotel of 1,850 rooms, a convention centre, shops, an ArtScience museum, a theatre and a casino. The casino opened in April 2010; the resort and SkyPark followed on 23–24 June.

Santiago Calatrava designed the Montjuïc Communications Tower, built between 1989 and 1992 for Telefónica to carry television coverage of that year's Summer Olympic Games in Barcelona. The white tower rises 136 metres in the Olympic park, a concrete spire meant to represent an athlete holding up the Olympic Flame. Its base is covered in trencadís, Gaudí's technique of mosaic made from broken pieces of tile. Because of the way it is oriented, the tower also acts as a giant sundial, with the Europa Square used to show the hour. One account counts it among Calatrava's most picturesque and sculptural works.

Santiago Calatrava, the Spanish neofuturist architect, designed the Museum of Tomorrow on the waterfront at Pier Maua in Rio de Janeiro. It occupies a 7,600-square-metre harbourside plaza, ringed by reflecting pools, and President Dilma Rousseff attended its opening on 17 December 2015. Calatrava wrote that the building should feel ethereal and seem almost to float on the water, evoking a ship, bird or plant. Movable screens on the roof respond to the sun's path. Seawater helps control the indoor temperature and tops up the pools. The museum was presented as a symbol of the port area's reurbanisation. Its main exhibition guides visitors through experiments and experiences in five areas: Cosmos, Earth, Anthropocene, Tomorrow, and finally Us.

Swiss architect Mario Botta designed Évry Cathedral, a Catholic church in Évry, a new town in Essonne. Paid for by over 200,000 donors, it was built between 1992 and 1995, opened that year and was consecrated in 1996, dedicated to Saint Corbinian; it is the only French cathedral both begun and completed during the 20th century. The building is a truncated cylinder under a sloping roof, its edge broken by trees whose colour changes with the seasons. Botta wrote that primary forms offer him clarity, a call to order within disorder. It looks all brick but is two reinforced concrete cylinders clad in standard-sized bricks, with passageways, stairs and technical rooms in the gap. The semicircular nave is laid out like a theatre, with rows on the main floor and two gallery levels, seating between 800 and 1,500 worshippers.

Jewel Changi Airport is a nature-themed shopping and entertainment complex, ringed by and joined to Changi's Terminals 1, 2 and 3 in Singapore. The idea was to join a marketplace with an urban park. Its glass and steel façade, shaped as a toroid, came from an architectural consortium headed by Moshe Safdie. The roof, a torus measuring 200 by 150 metres, is made of over 9,000 glass pieces, and a sloping oculus forms the mouth of the waterfall. Called the Rain Vortex, that waterfall drops 40 metres; no indoor waterfall anywhere is bigger or taller. The Forest Valley, among the biggest indoor gardens in Asia, climbs five storeys across about 22,000 square metres. The whole covers 135,700 square metres on ten levels, half of them underground. It officially opened on 18 October 2019, six months after a soft opening.

Pritzker Prize winner Zaha Hadid designed the London Aquatics Centre in 2004, before London had secured the 2012 Summer Olympics. It sits in Stratford, inside Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, and contains two 50-metre pools for swimming and one of 25 metres for diving. Since the design predated the successful bid, it had no spectator wings at first; these were added later to fit the expected audience, and during the Games it held 17,500. The 3,200-tonne roof is steel, the ceiling is made from 30,000 pieces of Red Louro wood, and 462 tonnes of concrete went into the six-board diving platform. The centre was finished in July 2011 at a final cost of £269 million. With the two temporary wings since removed, it seats 2,800 as standard, plus 1,000 extra for major events. Its public opening came on 1 March 2014.

The Glasshouse, on the Gateshead side of the Quayside in northern England, is an international centre for music education and concerts. Six teams were shortlisted and interviewed, and Foster and Partners was chosen unanimously; Buro Happold handled structure, Mott MacDonald acted as engineering consultants and Arup worked on acoustics. Its curved glass and stainless steel shell looks out on the Tyne Bridge, the Gateshead Millennium Bridge and the quaysides of both Newcastle and Gateshead. The shell wraps three structurally separate buildings without touching them, each insulated from the others against noise and vibration. Its performance spaces are a 1,700-seat hall, a 450-seat hall and the Northern Rock Foundation Hall for rehearsal and performance. Sage One was meant to be acoustically perfect, after Vienna's Musikverein. Planning and building cost over £70 million, mostly from National Lottery grants.

The Itamaraty Palace, also called the Palace of the Arches, is the headquarters of Brazil's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and it was inaugurated on 21 April 1970. Here he came back to the type used for Brasília's palaces: a glass box set between two concrete slabs with a colonnade. This time the columns run around every side rather than two, moving from a 'dipteral' to a 'peripteral' temple, with the upper slab lifted and the lower one meeting the reflecting pool. The classical round arch became the building's defining sign. Technically, the glass box and the arcades are two independent structures. The landscape designer Roberto Burle Marx created all of the palace's gardens. In 2007 the building was added to Brazil's National Historic Heritage list.

In Houston, the Rothko Chapel is both a chapel and the setting for fourteen black-hued paintings by Mark Rothko, who largely shaped its design, including the plan of an octagon within a Greek cross. He worked first with Howard Barnstone, then with Eugene Aubry, but died before the chapel was finished in 1971. The irregular brick octagon has stucco walls in grey or rose, and a skylight. Triptychs hang on three walls and single paintings on the remaining five. Since a 2020 renovation by Architecture Research Office with George Sexton Associates, the skylight's louvred diffuser has used 280 reflective aluminium blades, angled and spaced to light the paintings evenly. It entered the US National Register of Historic Places on 16 September 2000, and for its 50th anniversary in 2021 a $30 million restoration brought it closer to the original plan.

MARTa Herford is a museum of contemporary art in Herford, Germany. The idea for it took shape in 2000 and drew on the town's standing as a German centre for making furniture and home furnishings. The name is an acronym of Möbel, the German word for furniture, plus ART and Ambiente (ambience). Frank Gehry designed the building and Archimedes GmbH built it; work started in 2001, and the museum officially opened its doors on 7 May 2005. Its founding director was Jan Hoet, a well-known Belgian curator.

On Odderøya, in Norway's Kristiansand, Kilden Performing Arts Centre is a theatre and concert hall. It is home to Kilden Teater, Kilden Opera, Kilden Culture Venue and the Kristiansand Symphony Orchestra, a joint project never tried before. ALA Architects came into being in 2005, after a competition win for this building by Juho Grönholm, Antti Nousjoki, Janne Teräsvirta and Samuli Woolston. The Finnish office designed it with Norway's SMS Arkitekter; Brekke & Strand advised on acoustics, Arup shaped the concert hall's sound and AF Group was main contractor. A huge sloping wooden wall forms an overhang, a feature shared with Oodi and described as an ALA trademark. The building measures 16,000 square metres gross and 128,000 cubic metres in volume, cost close to 1.7 billion Norwegian kroner, and its concert hall seats 1,130. It officially opened on 6 January 2012.

Padre Pio Pilgrimage Church is one name for the Sanctuary of Saint Pio of Pietrelcina, a Catholic shrine at San Giovanni Rotondo, in Italy's Province of Foggia. Owned by the Capuchin order, it is dedicated to the Capuchin friar, priest and mystic known as Padre Pio. Renzo Piano, the Genoese architect, designed the new church, built between 1998 and 2004. It seats 6,500 worshippers, and 30,000 more can stand outside. The sanctuary also takes in the older church of Santa Maria delle Grazie and the convent where Padre Pio lived, with the new church directly behind them. In 2010 his body was moved to the newer church, where it lies enclosed in glass.

The Kunstmuseum Liechtenstein (Liechtenstein Museum of Fine Arts) serves as the state art museum in Vaduz. Meinrad Morger and Heinrich Degelo, with Christian Kerez, all Swiss architects, designed the building, which was officially given to the Principality of Liechtenstein in August 2000 as a millennium gift and completed that November. It is a closed 'black box' built of black basalt and tinted concrete, with river pebbles set into the outer surface. Inside, six exhibition rooms are grouped around two staircases placed diametrically opposite each other, and the plan opens diagonal views right through the building. In 2015 the Kunstmuseum gained a new exhibition building for the Hilti Art Foundation.

Alvar Aalto designed Helsinki's House of Culture, Kulttuuritalo, which is counted among his main works. It was built for Finnish Communist cultural organisations; Aalto worked without a fee and with full artistic freedom, and volunteers did much of the construction. Work started in 1955 and the building opened in 1958. It joins a concert hall and an office building through a block of lecture theatres, and a 60-metre canopy running along the street ties the parts together. The Finnish Council of State decided to protect the building in 1989. In July 2026 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site together with 12 other works by Aalto.

Zaryadye Park, Moscow's first new park in over 50 years, was designed by an international consortium led by Diller Scofidio + Renfro with Hargreaves Associates, Citymakers and BuroHappold Engineering, picked from 90 entries sent from 27 countries. It cost more than $480 million, and President Vladimir Putin and Mayor Sergey Sobyanin opened it on 9 September 2017. Its facilities are hidden beneath the landscape, which is split into four climate zones: forest, steppe, tundra and floodplain. The zones step down in terraces from northeast to southwest, each overlapping the next to create 14,000 square metres of enclosed, programmed space inside the land, so that nature and architecture work as one. The V-shaped Soaring Bridge reaches out over the water for 70 metres with no support; its load-bearing structure is concrete, its decorative parts metal and its deck wood.

The Edo-Tokyo Museum was the first museum built for the history of Tokyo. Kiyonori Kikutake won the commission through a closed competition held by Tokyo city hall. Its concrete exterior takes the form of a traditional rice storehouse and matches the height of Edo Castle, while its roof-like profile draws on the roofs of old Japanese temples and its whitish silver colour on Kyoto roofs catching the sun. Of its eight floors, one is underground and seven are lifted on four columns above an open-air plaza, from which a bright red escalator climbs to the main entrance on the third floor. The building cantilevers 119 feet beyond its legs on the north and south sides, and 126 springs spread through the overhang can absorb 3.5 inches of vertical movement, shielding the collection from vibration and earthquakes.

Le Corbusier named this 1958 apartment block in Berlin-Westend (Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf) Unité d'habitation 'Typ Berlin'; it follows his Unité d'Habitation concept and was later called the Corbusierhaus. It was planned in connection with Interbau 57, Berlin's 1957 international housing exhibition. Of the empty lots the city offered, he chose one between the stadium of the 1936 Olympics and a huge mound of rubble from wartime ruins. On the sandy ground, the ground-floor pilotis had to be doubled for stability. Built in béton brut, it belongs to the early phase of brutalism. A height Le Corbusier set at 226 cm became 250 cm, changing the whole structure and the flats. Seventeen floors hold 530 flats, against 337 in the 1952 Marseille Unité. The work was later removed from his oeuvre, and it has been a protected monument in Berlin since 1996.

David Chipperfield designed the James Simon Gallery, which opened in 2019 as the sixth building on Berlin's Museum Island and the last piece of his 1999 master plan for the island. It sits prominently on the site of Karl Friedrich Schinkel's Packhof, pulled down in 1938. Like the Louvre Pyramid, it receives and orients visitors and directs them to the main circuit. A wide staircase climbs in three flights to a raised plateau lined with 70 white concrete columns, nearly nine metres tall yet under 30 centimetres thick. The design pairs a stone base with a modern continuation of the colonnades by Friedrich August Stüler at the Alte Nationalgalerie. Inside are a 300-seat auditorium with pleated acoustic concrete walls, a media centre and a 600-square-metre temporary exhibition room. It is named after Henri James Simon, an art patron.

Imperial War Museum North, one of the Imperial War Museum's five branches, explores how modern conflicts affect people and society. The site overlooks the Manchester Ship Canal from Trafford Park, an industrial centre vital during the Second World War and therefore heavily bombed in the 1940 Manchester Blitz. Berlin-based Daniel Libeskind won the 1997 design competition with a 'constellation' of three interlocking shards, imagined as fragments of a globe broken by conflict. Representing air, earth and water, each holds a distinct part of the museum. The 55-metre air shard forms the entrance and has a viewing balcony over the canal, now closed. The 3,500-square-metre gallery floor in the earth shard curves down like the Earth from a notional 'North Pole' by the entrance. Budget cuts brought metal shards instead of concrete, dropped an auditorium and changed the exhibits.

Skuespilhuset, the Royal Danish Playhouse, is the Royal Danish Theatre's drama house in central Copenhagen. Built for spoken theatre, it complements the company's older stage of 1874 on Kongens Nytorv and the Copenhagen Opera House of 2004, which host ballet and opera. Its walls use a long, thin, deep-brown brick made for the project. A continuous glazed top storey of offices and actors' backstage rooms dominates the outside, with the stage tower above it as a dark, copper-clad cube. A glass foyer runs its full length along the water. Roughly 40% of it projects over the water, so the promenade swings around it on a raised walkway 150 metres long, of rough oak planks on crooked Venetian-style columns that make it seem to float. It won a RIBA European Award in 2008, and its chairs a Red Dot design award.

Kulturhuset, Stockholm's House of Culture, stands on Sergels torg's south side. Peter Celsing won the competition the city announced in 1965. Begun in 1966, it was inaugurated in 1974. From most sides its concrete structure dominates, but from the front the glass façade and slender concrete floor lines read as shelves open to the square. It was meant as a 'cultural oasis' in a new commercial centre, with an open library on the ground floor, a large theatre and exhibition space; the Stockholm Museum of Modern Art was to fill much of it but withdrew in 1969. Until 1983 it was the temporary home of the Riksdag while the parliament building was remodelled, and the building won the Kasper Salin Prize in 1972. It has been called a symbol of Stockholm and of modernism's growth in Sweden.

Danish architect-designer Arne Jacobsen created the SAS Royal Hotel for Scandinavian Airlines System, built from 1956 to 1960. King Frederik IX and Queen Ingrid opened it as the Royal Hotel on 1 July 1960. At 69.60 metres it was Copenhagen's first skyscraper and, until 1969, Denmark's tallest high-rise. Some call it the first designer hotel in the world: Jacobsen shaped everything from the building, furniture and fittings to the souvenir-shop ashtrays and the airport buses, and his Egg and Swan chairs were made for it. Its form, inspired by Lever House, sets a tall 'punch card' tower on a two-storey base, giving a sense of lightness. The tower's reinforced concrete frame carries a curtain wall of aluminium profiles with green and grey anodised glass. Only one room keeps its original design, with its green furniture and wooden wall panels.

The Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey, known as MARCO, sits in Monterrey's Centro district, beside the Macroplaza and the Barrio Antiguo. Mexican architect Ricardo Legorreta designed it in a minimalist postmodern style, and the building opened in 1991. The structure covers 16,000 square metres, of which 5,000 are given to exhibitions in 11 gallery halls, where artworks are shown under a balanced mix of daylight and artificial light. Outside there is a sculpture garden courtyard, and the Central Patio has a water mirror fountain. The museum also contains an auditorium, a gift shop and a restaurant.

Known as the New Cathedral, the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception of Mary stands in Managua, Nicaragua. Its predecessor was damaged in a 1972 earthquake, which levelled 90% of the city, and was judged beyond repair. Mexican architect Ricardo Legorreta designed the new building; work began around August 1991, and it was inaugurated on 4 September 1993, at an estimated cost of $4.5 million. Its many cupolas earned it the local nickname La Chichona, after chichas, a Nicaraguan Spanish slang word for breasts. It ranks with Mexico City's Camino Real Hotel and Guadalajara's IBM Factory among Legorreta's most famous works.

Japanese architect Toyo Ito designed Puebla's International Museum of the Baroque (Museo Internacional del Barroco, or MIB), a museum of Baroque art in Mexico that opened on 4 February 2016. The original project set out to conserve, research and share the many forms Baroque sensibility took, across art, culture, society, science and technology. Its first curatorial plan aimed to show how complex Baroque expression was in architecture, painting, sculpture, literature and other fields, and it included temporary exhibitions. After a change in the state administration, the museum reopened on 26 October 2019 with 'New Rites: Saints, Mourning, and Deities', an exhibition by the Mexican artist Mauro Terán.

Inaugurated on 28 September 2017, Lego House in Billund, Denmark, was designed by Bjarke Ingels Group. The 12,000-square-metre building, holding 25 million Lego bricks, stands near Legoland and the Lego Group's headquarters, where Billund's town hall once stood and a few metres from the workshop where the company started in 1932. It is meant to look like a stack of 21 white Lego bricks. Its modular spaces match a Lego brick's exact proportions, and so do the white ceramic tiles outside, sized like a classic 2x4 brick; they reflect light and keep the form calm, so as not to flood Billund with colour. The 21 rooms hang from a steel bridge, leaving the interiors open. Beyond its visitor centre role, it offers locals a shared urban space, and areas such as the roof terraces are free to enter.

Milan's Padiglione d'Arte Contemporanea (PAC), on via Palestro, has the Galleria d'Arte Moderna as its neighbour and faces the Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli. In 1947 the city, looking for somewhere new to show contemporary art, turned to the site of Villa Belgioiosa, which bombing had destroyed in 1943. Ignazio Gardella's design won a preliminary selection in March 1948, and the inauguration came in 1954. In 1993, while Italy was heavily engaged in fighting the Mafia, a bomb destroyed the building in the attack known as the Via Palestro massacre. Gardella then rebuilt the exhibition space to the original design, with key technical improvements, working with his son Jacopo Gardella; the rebuilt pavilion dates from 1996.

Tampere's main municipal library is also called Metso, the Finnish word for capercaillie, because seen from above it resembles that bird. Reima and Raili Pietilä designed it in an organic architecture style after a 1978 design contest, where their entry, Soidinmenot ('Lek mating'), won by unanimous decision. A visit to Ireland early in the process shaped their thinking, and the forms draw on Celtic patterns, animal shapes and glacial formations. Outside, the materials are granite, wiborgite, copper and glass; inside, the rooms are spread over three floors. Work on site started in 1983, and the doors opened to the public in August 1986. Between 2015 and 2017 a full renovation costing more than €11 million updated the building to meet current needs.

In Hamarøy, in Norway's Nordland county, this museum and educational centre presents the life and work of Knut Hamsun. Steven Holl was first approached in 1994. He took cues from the local landscape, from Norwegian traditions such as stave churches and roofs of sod, and from Hamsun's books, above all Hunger (1890) and Mysteries (1892). Holl described the centre as giving a Hamsun character architectural form. His first choice was a site close to the house in Hamsund where Hamsun was a boy, but local officials moved the project 5 km east, to Presteid, where the writer spent much of his childhood with an uncle. The centre was finished on 4 August 2009, 150 years after Hamsun's birth, and its exhibition opened in June 2010. Its design has stirred debate and won architecture awards at home and abroad.

Robert Mallet-Stevens built this early modernist house between 1923 and 1927 for Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles, patrons of the arts, on the hills overlooking Hyères, in the Var in southeastern France. Building work took three years, and the project came to include a triangular Cubist garden by Gabriel Guevrekian. The furniture was bought or specially made, some by Mallet-Stevens himself, whose "Transat" armchair was created for the swimming pool, and other pieces by designers such as Eileen Gray, Pierre Chareau, Charlotte Perriand and Jean Prouvé. Works by Brâncuși, Giacometti, Mondrian and Braque were among the art. Man Ray's film Les Mystères du Château de Dé gives the villa a prominent role. The Italian Army took it over in 1940 and turned it into a hospital. Today it is an arts centre that hosts special exhibitions.

Jørn Utzon, the architect of the Sydney Opera House, designed this centre as his last building, working with his son Kim, who drew up the final construction drawings. He did not intend a museum but a meeting place where architecture students could talk through their ideas for the future. It stands by the Limfjord in Aalborg, where Utzon grew up, and was finished in 2008, the year of his death. Several separate buildings are grouped around a courtyard raised on a platform. The auditorium and the boathall on the harbour side, and the library turned toward the park and the city, carry tall, curved, highly reflective roofs, while lower roofs cover the exhibition and workshop areas. The tent-like rooms recall Utzon's years in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. An archive keeps his original drawings.

At Oberseestraße 60 in Berlin's Alt-Hohenschönhausen district, the Lemke House, also called Mies van der Rohe Haus, was the last house Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed in Germany before leaving for the United States in 1938. Several schemes came first, most of them for two storeys, and building started in the summer of 1932 at a cost of 16,000 Reichsmarks. The house is an L in plan, simple and modest, yet it suited the needs of a childless couple. Its walls are red, charcoal-fired brick under a flat roof. Some of the furnishings came from Mies's studio, and Lilly Reich, his partner, designed others. Berlin's magistrate added the house to the district monument list in 1977, and it was renovated between 2000 and 2002. Today it is a pavilion for exhibitions of modern art.

This museum in Alstahaug Municipality, Norway, is devoted to Petter Dass, a priest and poet. Its building is the work of the Snøhetta architecture office. Work on the new museum and a car park began in September 2005; after the opening was put off several times in 2007, the museum opened its doors on 20 October 2007. Building it cost about 90 million kroner, paid for by the municipality, the county municipality and the state together with private donors. When Alstahaug was picked in 1999 as Nordland county's millennium site, the museum played a central part. The Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage protects the courtyard, Alstahaug Church, the cemetery and the buildings.

Also called the Wacoal Art Center, Spiral is a mixed-use building in Aoyama, Tokyo, designed by Fumihiko Maki for the lingerie company Wacoal and finished in 1985. Shops, beauty salons, cafes, restaurants and bars share it with exhibition spaces and a multipurpose hall. Its main feature is a spiral ramp, 15 metres across, that seems to float as it wraps around the gallery at the back and rises to the second floor. On the street, an aluminium and glass facade mirrors the jumbled character of its surroundings. In 1987 it received the R.S. Reynolds Memorial Award from the American Institute of Architects, and in 2012 the Japan Institute of Architects gave it the JIA 25 Years Award.

Hans Poelzig designed this Frankfurt headquarters for IG Farben in the New Objectivity style, and it was completed in 1931. It was the largest building put up in the Weimar Republic and stayed Europe's biggest office complex until the 1950s. The board picked Poelzig's scheme, a long, curved main block with six cross wings. The block runs 250 metres, its wings joined by a curved central corridor, so the offices get daylight and fresh air without the closed courtyards common in big office buildings of the time. Travertine faces the steel frame, and horizontal window bands stress the curve. After American forces took Frankfurt in March 1945, it housed Allied and American military administration. Dissing+Weitling won the competition to adapt it for university use, and it reopened on 26 October 2001 as the first major part of the Westend Campus.

The first church on this site dated from the 1890s and was badly damaged by bombing in 1943. Egon Eiermann won the competition for its replacement and, in both of his entries, wanted the ruined spire pulled down for an entirely new building. Public protest, which called the tower the "heart of Berlin", led him to revise the design and keep it. Built from 1959 to 1963, the new group pairs an octagonal church with a hexagonal belfry on a plateau 100 by 40 metres, and the old spire's ground floor became a memorial hall. The church walls are a concrete honeycomb holding 21,292 stained glass inlays by Gabriel Loire, inspired by the glass at Chartres Cathedral and mostly blue, with touches of ruby red, emerald green and yellow. Berliners call it "der hohle Zahn", the hollow tooth.

In 1976 Fariborz Sahba won a worldwide competition for this temple, chosen from 45 entrants. He picked the lotus because it is sacred to several of India's religions, Hinduism and Buddhism among them, and in some traditions stands for purity. A rule set by ʻAbdu'l-Bahá requires every Baháʼí House of Worship to be circular and nine-sided. Its 27 free-standing concrete petals rise in threes from nine arches, in three rings around a central hall. Outside, they wear white Pentelic marble from Greece; inside, the white concrete was hammered by hand. Designed to cool itself like a desert wind tower, the building draws air over its pools, into the basement, up through the hall and out at the crown. Nine pools stand for the lotus leaves, so the flower seems to float. It was dedicated on 24 December 1986.

Built for the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City, the Palacio de los Deportes was made for the basketball tournament but planned from the start as a multipurpose arena. Félix Candela designed it with Enrique Castañeda Tamborel and Antonio Peyri. The plan is circular, under a dome with a square pattern that spans 120 metres (380 feet) and covers 27,000 square metres. The dome is made of hyperbolic paraboloids of tubular aluminium, covered in waterproof plywood sheathed in copper and carried on huge steel arches. The construction company ICA built it between 15 October 1966 and 13 September 1968, finishing a month before the Games. It first held 22,370 people, 7,370 of them in removable seats. In the 1990s a series of changes adjusted its acoustics.

At the heart of the Nezu Museum is the art that Nezu Kaichirō (1860–1940) collected privately: pre-modern works from Japan and East Asia. The museum closed in 2006 for large-scale renovation and renewal and reopened in autumn 2009 in an entirely new building designed by Kengo Kuma. Its holdings number over 7,400 objects; the Japanese government has named seven of them National Treasures, 88 Important Cultural Properties and 94 Important Art Objects. The museum is also known for its Japanese garden, where irises are planted, and each year from April to May a special exhibition is timed to their flowering. A 2010 Mainichi Art Award was given for the Nezu Museum.

Home to Oslo's city council, its administration and other municipal bodies, Oslo City Hall was built between 1931 and 1950, with a pause during the Second World War. Arnstein Arneberg and Magnus Poulsson won in 1918 with a design that clearly drew on Stockholm City Hall. By their final draft of 1930 it had changed a great deal under the influence of functionalism, most visibly through two added office towers, which rise 63 and 66 metres. The walls are red brick, laid with bricks larger than was usual at the time and close in size to medieval ones. The main hall, decorated by Henrik Sørensen and Alf Rolfsen, measures 31 by 39 metres and rises about 21 metres. By the 1950 opening the style had fallen out of favour. The Nobel Peace Prize ceremony is held here every December.

Hector Guimard designed the Paris Metro's first set of station entrances from 1900 to 1913. Mostly dating from 1900, his cast iron and glass designs and the lettering he made for them produced what came to be called the Métro style and helped popularise Art Nouveau. He chose cast iron fixed in concrete over stone, which kept costs down and suited the flowing lines, and painted it green to look like weathered brass. The parts were standardised: railing cartouches with an "M", and signs saying "Métropolitain", or "Métro" where the entrance was narrow. At many entrances, the sign is held between two sinuous stalks, likened to lily of the valley, each topped by a red-orange globe lamp. Guimard's work for the Métro ended in 1904, when his Opéra station design was rejected. Eighty-six entrances survive as protected historical monuments.

Rio de Janeiro's cathedral is dedicated to the city's patron saint, Saint Sebastian. Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca gave it a modern design that takes its cue from Mayan pyramids. Built from 1964 to 1979, it took over as seat of the Archdiocese from a series of churches used as cathedrals since 1676, the last and best known being the 18th-century Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of the Ancient See, now called the Old Cathedral. The building is a cone 75 metres high, measuring 96 metres across inside and 106 metres outside. Its interior covers 8,000 square metres, with 5,000 seats and standing room for 20,000. Four straight-edged stained glass windows run 64 metres from floor to ceiling.

No museum in the world devoted to one civilization is larger than the Grand Egyptian Museum. Entrants from 82 countries submitted 1,557 designs, making its competition the second largest architectural contest ever held. The Irish practice Heneghan Peng Architects, led by Róisín Heneghan and Shi-Fu Peng, won. The building, a chamfered triangle, stands 2 kilometres northwest of the pyramids, close to a motorway interchange, and its north and south walls line up with the pyramids of Khufu and Menkaure. A plaza planted with date palms fronts a facade of translucent alabaster. Inside, the 10,000 square metre Great Hall, under a glass roof behind a transparent front, keeps the pyramids in view. Announced in 1992 and started in 2005, the museum was completed in 2023 for $1.2 billion and officially opened on 1 November 2025.

Designed by the Argentine-American architect César Pelli, the Petronas Towers in Kuala Lumpur are two linked supertall skyscrapers of 88 storeys, 451.9 metres high. They were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 until Taipei 101 overtook them in 2004. Because importing steel was so costly, they are built mostly of reinforced concrete of very high strength. The steel and glass facade echoes motifs from Islamic art, and the cross section takes its shape from a Rub el Hizb, with circular sectors added to gain office space. Concrete cores 23 metres square and an outer ring of super columns set far apart carry the slender towers and leave 560,000 square metres of offices free of columns. A two-level skybridge joins them at the 41st and 42nd floors, 170 metres up. The design won Pelli the Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Taipei 101 was officially the world's tallest building from its opening day, 31 December 2004, until the Burj Khalifa passed it in 2009. C. Y. Lee's postmodernist and neo-futurist design evokes traditional Asian aesthetics through a modern structure of industrial materials. The main tower is made of eight stacked sections, each eight floors high; in Chinese-speaking cultures, eight is linked with prosperity, abundance and good fortune. These blocks recall a pagoda, a bamboo stalk and a stack of ancient Chinese ingots or money boxes. With a major fault line 200 metres away, outrigger trusses every eight floors tie the core columns to the outer ones. A 660-tonne steel pendulum by Motioneering, hung between the 92nd and 88th floors, offsets sway from strong gusts, and double chamfered corners sharply cut crosswind movement. It gained LEED Platinum certification in 2011.

Designed by Nikolai Nikitin, Moscow's Ostankino Tower rises 540.1 metres; as of 2026 no free-standing structure in Europe is taller, and it ranks 15th in the world. It was the first such structure to pass 500 metres, and it marked half a century since the October Revolution. Nikitin proposed reinforced concrete, citing a successful similar tower in Stuttgart finished in 1956, and he strengthened the concrete frame with about 150 taut steel ropes. Nikitin's design had a very shallow foundation, only 4.6 metres deep. Arches between the supports, a glazed cylinder under the trunk for technical services and broadcast studios, and windows in the upper cone give it the look of a rocket. Work began in 1959. A fire on 27 August 2000 engulfed the Seventh Heaven restaurant and damaged the structure; only 19 of those cables came through intact.

Pakistan's national mosque, in the capital Islamabad, came out of a 1969 international competition in which architects from 17 countries sent in 43 proposals; the Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay won. Instead of a usual dome, the building takes the shape of a Bedouin tent, with eight-sided sloping shell roofs forming a triangular prayer hall for 10,000 worshippers. Four concrete girders carry the main hall, and four 90-metre minarets, inspired by Turkish architecture, stand around it. Inside, white marble lines the hall, which has a Turkish-style chandelier and mosaics and calligraphy by the Pakistani artist Sadequain. The mosque stands at the northern end of Faisal Avenue, at the city's northern edge, below the Margalla Hills, the most westerly foothills of the Himalayas. From 1986 until 1993 no mosque in the world was larger.

Kohn Pedersen Fox designed this supertall tower in Shanghai's Pudong district for the developer Mori Building Company. It holds offices, hotels and conference rooms, with a shopping mall on the ground floor. Topped out at 492 metres on 14 September 2007, it was the world's second tallest building on completion after Taipei 101, the tallest by roof height alone, and the tallest in mainland China. Its most distinctive feature is the opening at the top. The first design had a circle 46 metres across, to ease wind pressure and to recall the Chinese mythological image of the sky as a circle. In October 2005 KPF proposed a trapezoidal hole instead, which the architects said was cheaper and easier to build. The tower is nicknamed "the bottle opener". The CTBUH named it the best tall building completed in 2008.

At 632 metres and 128 storeys, the Shanghai Tower in Lujiazui, Pudong, is the tallest building in China and the world's third tallest to its architectural top. The American firm Gensler designed it, with the Shanghainese architect Jun Xia as design lead. Nine cylindrical buildings are stacked inside an inner glass skin; between this and a twisting outer skin lie nine public zones, each with its own atrium of gardens, cafés, restaurants, shops and city views. The outer facade turns 120° as it climbs, meant to cut wind loads by 24%, so the tower used a quarter less structural steel than a conventional one of its height. The double glass skin is designed to reduce air conditioning, and heating and cooling draw on geothermal sources. Work began on 29 November 2008; it topped out on 4 August 2013.

The library's job is to gather, protect and promote Kosovo's documentary and intellectual heritage and to make it available. Its present building, by the Croatian architect Andrija Mutnjaković, was inaugurated on 25 November 1982. It covers 16,500 square metres and takes light from above through 99 domes of various sizes, while a metal fishing net, with its own architectural symbolism, wraps the whole exterior. The biggest dome crowns the high ceiling of the hall, bringing in plenty of daylight over a floor of mixed marble mosaic. Mutnjaković meant the building to blend Byzantine and Islamic forms; others read it as a reply to the impersonality of the International Style, joining modern means with regional and rural traditions, or call it Modern-Metabolist. Inside are reading rooms for 300 and 100 people, a 150-seat amphitheatre and room for about two million volumes.

Graz built its Kunsthaus for its year as European Capital of Culture in 2003, and the museum, which shows contemporary art from the 1960s on, is now one of the Austrian city's architectural landmarks. It was designed by Sir Peter Cook and Colin Fournier. An example of blob architecture, it wears a skin of iridescent blue acrylic panels that double as photovoltaic panels. Its form, so unlike the buildings around it, earned the nickname "Friendly Alien". It takes in the facade of the Iron House, an 1848 structure with an iron frame. Behind the acrylic glass on the east side is the BIX: 930 fluorescent lamps, each dimmable on its own, which turn the facade into a big screen for films and animations, a "communicative display skin". It was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2004.

The National Gallery of Australia is the country's national art museum, with a collection of over 166,000 works. The 1968 design competition went to Colin Madigan of Edwards Madigan Torzillo and Partners, though doubts over the final site meant no design could be settled then. Work began in 1973, and Queen Elizabeth II opened the gallery in 1982. Its style is late 20th-century Brutalism: angular masses and raw concrete, ringed by sculpture gardens of Australian native plants and trees. A triangle governs the geometry, seen most clearly in the grids of the coffered ceilings and in the floor tiles of the main level. The structure is mainly reinforced bush-hammered concrete, which at first was also the finish of the inside walls. In November 2007 the High Court and National Gallery Precinct was entered on Australia's National Heritage List.

The Kyoto International Conference Center, shortened to ICC Kyoto, is a large conference facility at Takaragaike in Kyoto's Sakyō ward, and it is where the Kyoto Protocol was signed. Sachio Otani designed it around an unusual hexagonal framework, so it has few vertical walls or columns. It opened in 1966, and an addition followed in 1973. The building is a rare surviving example of Metabolism in Japan, since the newer and better-known Nakagin Capsule Tower Building was pulled down in 2022. Today the whole facility offers meeting space totalling 156,000 m²: the main Conference Hall, with a large room for 2,000 people and several smaller rooms, an Annex Hall for 1,500, and an Event Hall. The Prince Kyoto Takaragaike Hotel stands nearby.

The Basilica of the Madonna delle Lacrime, a 20th-century Catholic shrine to Mary, dominates the skyline on the approach to Ortigia in Syracuse, Sicily. Michel Andrault and Pierre Parat won an international competition for its design, and Riccardo Morandi was the main engineer. Building took from 1966 to 1994, and along the way a crypt, probably a paleo-Christian mausoleum, turned up in the foundations; it now lies in the church's lower rooms. The building was planned larger and cut back by some 30 metres, ending at 103 metres high. One reading sees a giant teardrop hitting the earth; others mock it as an upside-down ice-cream cone. It honours a claimed miracle of 1953, when a plaster image of the Madonna was said to have wept. Pope John Paul II raised it to a minor basilica in 2002.

In Yerevan, the Cascade is a monumental complex where fountains, sculptures, terraces and exhibition halls line a staircase climbing over many levels. It links the city centre with the higher ground of the Kanaker-Zeytun district and is an important part of the axis set out in Alexander Tamanyan's master plan. The idea first appeared in that plan, drawn up in the 1920s, which pictured terraces, waterfalls and flower beds rising to the northern hills of Kanaker. In the early 1970s Jim Torosyan, with Aslan Mkhitaryan and Sargis Gurzadyan, began a new design. Building started in 1980 but halted in the late 1980s, after the 1988 Armenian earthquake, the First Nagorno-Karabakh War and the end of the Soviet Union. Five main terraces, joined by stairs and escalators, stretch about 302 metres. Its stone is travertine and milky white tuff.

Part of the Israel Museum in Jerusalem's Givat Ram neighbourhood, the Shrine of the Book holds the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Aleppo Codex and other texts. Frederick John Kiesler, Armand Phillip Bartos and Gezer Heller spent seven years designing it. Two-thirds of the structure lies below ground under a white dome, mirrored in the surrounding pool, and a black basalt wall stands opposite. According to one interpretation, the building's colours and shapes come from the Scroll of the War of the Sons of Light Against the Sons of Darkness, with the dome as light and the wall as darkness. Each scroll is displayed for three to six months and then moved to a special storeroom to "rest" from exposure. Israeli architects objected that the commission went to architects who were Jews but not Israelis.

Laid out where a Citroën car works once stood and named after the firm's founder, André Citroën, this 14-hectare public park lies on the Seine's left bank in Paris's 15th arrondissement. Its 1992 opening made it the biggest new park in the city in over a hundred years. The landscape designers Alain Provost and Gilles Clément shaped it with the architects Patrick Berger, Jean-Paul Viguier and Jean-François Jodry. At the core is a rectangular lawn measuring about 273 by 85 metres. At the east end, dancing fountains play on a paved area between two greenhouse pavilions of exotic and Mediterranean plants. On the north side are six Serial Gardens, each tied to a metal, a planet, a weekday, a state of water and a sense, plus a Garden in Movement whose wild grasses respond to the wind at different speeds.

Kamppi Chapel, also called the Chapel of Silence, is meant as somewhere to quieten down and pause for a moment of silence in one of the busiest parts of Helsinki. It is ecumenical, welcoming people of any faith, background or philosophy of life. Designed by Kimmo Lintula, Mikko Summanen and Niko Sirola of K2S Architects, it was built as part of the World Design Capital programme in 2012, and the design took an International Architecture Award in 2010. Inside and out it is very austere, simple and largely neutral, a little like a multi-faith prayer room. No regular church services are held there. Visitors came at once: about 250,000 by January 2013, and the 500,000th a year after that. CNN called the chapel an architectural landmark.

Rashtrapati Bhavan, the "President's House", is the Indian President's official home, standing at the western end of Rajpath on Raisina Hill in New Delhi. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed it, and building ran from 1912 to 1929. Lutyens kept the design broadly classical, with colours and details taken from Indo-Saracenic architecture. Twelve massive, unevenly spaced columns line the east front, crowned by the Delhi Order, a one-off order of Lutyens' own invention, whose capitals mix acanthus leaves with four hanging Indian bells. Ornament on the drum below the main dome recalls the railings of early Buddhist stupas like Sanchi. A thin chhajja, projecting 2.4 metres where a classical frieze would be, casts deep shadow and keeps harsh sun and monsoon rain off the windows. No head of state has a larger official residence by floor area.

Rising 309.6 metres over 71 storeys in Tianhe, Guangzhou, the Pearl River Tower is a neofuturistic skyscraper built around clean technology. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill handled its architecture and engineering, with Gordon Gill and Adrian D. Smith as architects. Ground was broken on 8 September 2006, and the tower was finished in March 2011. The designers aimed for a zero-energy building in four steps: reduction, absorption, reclamation and generation. The broadest face is set square to the prevailing wind, and the form channels air through four large wind turbines, which can produce up to 15 times the energy of ordinary freestanding ones. In the double-skin facade, the outer layer lets solar heat in while the inner layer blocks solar gain. The finished 212,165 m² tower uses about 40% of the energy usual for a building its size.

Inside the Moorilla winery on Hobart's Berriedale peninsula in Tasmania, MONA, the Museum of Old and New Art, is the biggest privately paid-for museum in the Southern Hemisphere. It opened officially in January 2011. From the street the one-storey building seems dwarfed by its surroundings, but a spiral staircase inside descends to three bigger levels of maze-like galleries cut into the peninsula's cliffs. By one account, it was put mostly underground to spare the historic setting of two houses on the site designed by Roy Grounds. It has no windows and feels ominous on purpose. Visitors see the art while working back up toward the surface, a route some have set against the downward spiral of New York's Guggenheim Museum. Most arrive on the ferry up the Derwent. It won the 2012 Sir Zelman Cowen Award for Public Architecture.

The Jin Mao Tower is a 420.5-metre, 88-storey skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. Inside are shops, offices and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai, which begins on the 53rd floor and was the world's highest hotel when the tower was completed. The Chicago firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it. Its postmodern form grows more complex with height and borrows from traditional Chinese buildings such as the tiered pagoda, stepping back gently in a steady rhythm. The proportions turn on the number 8, linked with prosperity in Chinese culture: above a 16-storey base come 16 segments, each one-eighth shorter than the base. An octagonal concrete core is ringed by 8 composite supercolumns and 8 steel columns. Its foundations stand on 1,062 steel piles driven 83.5 metres down, at the time the longest steel piles ever used for a building on land.

Built, like its Hiroshima counterpart, as somewhere to remember the dead of the 1945 atomic bombing and pray for them, the hall gathers photographs, memoirs and personal accounts. Akira Kuryu was the architect, and construction ran from November 2000 to December 2002. Below ground are a reference area and a big conference room, an anteroom where a bank of monitors shows the victims' photographs, and a stylised Remembrance Hall where 12 pillars of light express hope for peace. Above ground, the memorial's top is chiefly a basin of water edged with trees, and the same 12 pillars of light rise up through it. After dark, 70,000 fibre optic lights shine across the water's surface, standing for the victims. On an upper level, a shorter tour offers diary excerpts and a place to look down into the Remembrance Hall.

This museum honours the people killed in the Nanjing Massacre, carried out by Japan's Imperial Army in and around the city, then China's capital, after it fell on 13 December 1937. It stands at Jiangdongmen, in the southwest of downtown Nanjing, near a mass burial site known as the "pit of ten thousand people". The Nanjing Municipal Government built it in 1985 to commemorate the massacre's three hundred thousand victims. The design is credited to Qi Kang, with a first phase from 1983 to 1985 and a second in 1995, when the memorial was enlarged and renovated. Records, objects, architecture, sculpture and video show what happened. Its three main parts are outdoor exhibits, a shelter over victims' skeletal remains, and a tomb-like exhibition hall, half underground, with over 1,000 items. The site covers about 28,000 square metres.

Seoullo 7017, or Seoul Skygarden, is a linear park raised on a former highway overpass in Seoul. Its path, about a kilometre long and planted with 24,000 plants, resembles New York City's High Line. The Dutch firm MVRDV designed it, and it opened in May 2017. The overpass, closed in 2015, crosses Seoul Station on a diagonal 17 metres above the street. The "70" in the name refers to 1970, when the flyover was dedicated; the "17" marks both the number of walkways linked to it and its 2017 opening. The park holds gardens, terraces and exhibitions, with plants of 228 species promised. Mayor Park Won-soon pushed the US$52 million project as a companion to the Cheonggyecheon Stream restoration organised under an earlier mayor, Lee Myung-bak. Rogier van der Heide designed its deep blue night lighting.

No cultural facility in Taiwan is larger than the National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts, which is also the world's largest performing arts theatre under one roof, and the first performing arts venue of national rank in southern Taiwan. Mecanoo secured the rights to design and build it in 2007, and the Dutch architect Francine Houben designed the main building. It holds four indoor halls: a 2,236-seat Opera House, a 1,981-seat Concert Hall, a 1,209-seat Playhouse and a 434-seat Recital Hall. Houben drew on the Weiwuying banyan tree grove, so the public can enter from every side, and the four halls and an outdoor theatre are joined by Banyan Plaza. A curved roof of 35,000 square metres, made from 4,500 aluminium alloy panels, covers it all. Shipbuilding techniques shaped the curves, a nod to Kaohsiung Harbor and its shipbuilding past.

The Standard Bank Centre in Johannesburg, nicknamed the Hanging Building, is a 139-metre skyscraper built between 1966 and 1968. Hubert Petschnigg of Austria and Helmut Hentrich of Germany planned it with the engineer Ove Arup; their challenge was finding a roomy square in the crowded central business district on which to anchor an office building. To use as little space as possible, they chose a "hanging" design. Once the central core was up, the floors were hung from cantilevered arms, starting at the top and working down floor by floor. A slewing crane made for the job lifted and placed a quarter of each floor at a time. Apart from the concrete core, Concor built it of steel, glass and precast slabs of reinforced concrete. The offices are 9.7 metres wide, and hanging them removes the need for pillars.

Three slender towers stand on a promontory in the Persian Gulf at Kuwait City. They are the last of six groups in the Kuwait Water Towers network of 34 towers, and they look unlike the other five. The Danish architect Malene Bjørn designed them within a water supply scheme led by the Swedish engineering firm VBB. The Amir chose this design from three shown to him out of ten. The main tower, 187 metres tall, holds two spheres. All three, of reinforced and prestressed concrete, were built from 1971 to 1976, and the main tower opened to visitors on 1 March 1979. Around 41,000 enamelled steel discs in eight shades of blue, green and grey clad the spheres, recalling historic mosques with tiled domes. In 1980 the water tower system was among the Aga Khan Award's first winners.

Over 66,000 works spanning 30 centuries fill the Museo Soumaya: Pre-Hispanic sculpture from Mesoamerica, Mexican art of the 19th and 20th centuries, and European old masters and modern Western artists, among them Rodin, Dalí, Murillo and Tintoretto. Fernando Romero, a Mexican architect and son-in-law of Carlos Slim, designed the new building at Plaza Carso in Nuevo Polanco, working with Ove Arup and Frank Gehry on the engineering. It cost $70 million and opened in 2011. The six-storey block rises 46 metres under a skin of 16,000 hexagonal aluminium tiles. Its weight rests on an exoskeleton of 28 curved steel columns and seven ring beams. A narrow entrance gives onto a large white gallery, each floor has a different shape, and the open top floor is lit by the sun. No collection of Rodin casts outside France is larger.

Palacio Salvo stands where 18 de Julio Avenue meets Plaza Independencia, in central Montevideo, Uruguay. Mario Palanti, an Italian immigrant based in Buenos Aires, designed this eclectic skyscraper and used a similar scheme for his Palacio Barolo. Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy inspired both, and Palanti's original idea was to join Montevideo and Buenos Aires with a "bridge of light" over the Río de la Plata, using the lighthouses on their domes. On completion the Salvo was the world's tallest reinforced concrete structure, and for a short time no building in Latin America stood higher. Its style blends Renaissance references, Gothic echoes and Neoclassical details, and its outline has become a symbol of the city. It was meant to be a hotel, but offices and private homes filled it instead. Uruguay listed it as a National Historical Monument in 1996.

Toba Sea-Folk Museum in Toba, Mie Prefecture, Japan, is devoted to the fishing traditions of the area. It began in 1971 as a private museum, moved to its present site in 1992, and in 2017 became a public museum run by the city. The buildings, designed by Naitō Hiroshi, were named in 1998 among the 100 Select Instances of Public Architecture chosen by what was then the Ministry of Construction. As of 31 March 2018 the collection held about 61,840 items, among them some ninety wooden boats from across Japan and the country's fullest set of material on the Ama. A group of 6,879 fishing tools from Ise Bay, the Shima Peninsula and the Kumano Sea is jointly listed as an Important Tangible Folk Cultural Property. Seven themes shape the displays, from sea-folk faith to sea pollution and wooden boats.

A Sino-British Club campaign to re-establish a civic centre led to Hong Kong City Hall. It rose in the late 1950s on 10,000 square metres of land newly reclaimed from the sea, some 200 metres from the first city hall. The original design was by Professor Gordon Brown, the first head of the architecture department at Hong Kong University, and his team, among them Patricia O'Reilly Mayne; the British architects Ronald Phillips and Alan Fitch completed it for HK$20 million. Governor Sir Robert Brown Black attended the 1960 foundation stone ceremony and presided at the opening on 2 March 1962. Its two steel-and-concrete blocks and gardens are arranged as one whole along a central axis. Its clean, plain geometry is International style. In 2022 it became Hong Kong's youngest declared monument, and the first from after the Second World War.

Morpheus, a neo-futurist hotel in Macau run by Melco Resorts & Entertainment, was designed by Zaha Hadid Architects. The firm faced a tight rectangular footprint of 6,850 square metres on a site that already had foundations. Its answer, drawn from Chinese jade artifacts, is a twisting exoskeleton that holds up two towers and several skybridges. This steel grid carries both gravity and sideways loads, which cuts the need for internal columns and opens up large spaces inside; it was the first building in Asia to do without a single internal column. Work began in 2014; the steel plates were welded into shape at a shipbuilding yard in Guangdong. Opened in June 2018 after a US$1.1 billion build, it rises 153.7 metres and holds 772 rooms, nine being two-storey sky villas. TIME called it the world's first free-form exoskeleton-bound high-rise.

Lanyang Museum, in Yilan County, Taiwan, tells the story of the local area. The firm Artech was given the design and construction in April 2000, and the team under Kris Yao took its cue from the cuestas seen along the Beiguan Coast. Borrowing their geometry, the building seems to rise out of the ground the way those landforms do: its roof lifts from the earth at 20 degrees and meets a wall climbing at 70 degrees. Inside, exhibits cover the landscape of Yilan, from mountains and plains to the sea. The museum opened officially on 16 October 2010. Two years later it received The International Architecture Award, given by The Chicago Athenaeum together with a European centre for architecture and urban studies.

Taipei Performing Arts Center is a performance venue in Shilin District, Taipei, Taiwan. OMA won the competition to build it in January 2009, and the building was designed by David Gianotten and Rem Koolhaas of the Office for Metropolitan Architecture. Construction started in 2012. After a trial opening between March and May 2022, the center opened officially on 2 July 2022. Its parts include a cube-shaped structure, a playhouse shaped like a sphere that seats 800, the Grand Theater, an asymmetrical building seating 1,500, and the Blue Box, a 500-seat room for experimental performance.

Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art is in the Hannam-dong area of Seoul, South Korea, and the Samsung Foundation of Culture runs it. It is counted among the three leading private art museums in the country. The museum comes in two parts, one for traditional Korean art and the other for contemporary art. Swiss architect Mario Botta designed the first part, while the second is the work of French architect Jean Nouvel together with Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas. Museum 2 (M2) shows modern and contemporary art by Korean and foreign artists, with permanent exhibition spaces for figures such as Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol and Mark Rothko.

National Gallery Singapore occupies two national monuments in the Civic District, the former Supreme Court and the former City Hall. Their 64,000 square metres make it the largest museum in Singapore, with more than 9,000 works of art from Singapore and Southeast Asia. After an international competition, studioMilou was appointed in May 2008, with CPG Consultants, to design and build it. Because both are protected, the façades, the Surrender Chamber and some other parts had to stay as they were, though new roof and basement floors were allowed. The design ties the two buildings together at roof level with a draped linear canopy on tree-like columns; bridges and a new basement also connect them. Work began in January 2011, the gallery opened on 24 November 2015, and it won Design of the Year at the 2015 President's Design Award.

Pinnacle@Duxton is 50-storey public housing in central Singapore. Its design came from a worldwide competition, something no other Housing and Development Board project had, which drew 227 entries from 32 countries. The winners were two Singapore firms, ARC Studio Architecture + Urbanism working with RSP Architects Planners & Engineers. Seven linked towers make up the scheme, together the tallest public housing in the world. Sky gardens 500 metres long join them on the 26th and 50th floors, the longest yet built on skyscrapers, with jogging tracks, playgrounds and places to rest and look out. Buyers could choose layouts with balconies, planter boxes or bay windows, and the light inner walls can be moved. Construction was fully pre-cast. In 2010 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat named it the best tall building in Asia and Australasia.

Kuala Lumpur International Airport, at Sepang, Malaysia, was formally opened on 27 June 1998 by Tuanku Ja'afar, Malaysia's tenth Yang di-Pertuan Agong, shortly before the 1998 Commonwealth Games. Japanese architect Kisho Kurokawa designed Terminal 1, putting the stress on daylight. The Main Terminal Building lies between the two runways and covers 390,000 square metres beneath 39 square roof units, a system that leaves room for later growth. With spans of 38.4 metres set along a grid, Kurokawa's abstract, symbolic design brings Islamic geometry and advanced technology together with ideas of the tropical rainforest, and a natural patch of rainforest grows at the heart of the terminal. The airport earned its architect the Dedalo-Minosse International Prize (Grand Prix) in 2003. Every year since 2004 it has held the United Nations' Green Globe 21 certification, which no other airport has received.

Sumet Jumsai designed the Robot Building in Bangkok for the Bank of Asia, whose directors wanted a building that expressed how banking was being modernised and computerised.
