Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and the engineer Joaquim Cardozo did the structural work. It stands on the Three Powers Plaza (Praça dos Três Poderes) with the Palácio do Planalto, the presidential palace, and the National Congress. Like Niemeyer's other Brasília buildings designed by 1960, among them the Congress, the Cathedral and the Palácio da Alvorada, it was experimental and shares design elements with them. Pillars along its sides lift the building slightly off the ground, which makes the whole look light, and Cardozo's calculations let its foundations stay thin, barely touching the ground. In front stands Alfredo Ceschiatti's statue A Justiça (Justice), carved in 1961. IPHAN declared it national heritage in 2007, the year Niemeyer turned 100.

The Palmach Museum in Ramat Aviv, Israel, honours the Palmach, the strike force of the Haganah, the underground defence group of the years before the state, which was later merged into the Israel Defense Forces. It opened in 2000 and marks the Palmach's part in founding the State of Israel. The Israeli architects Zvi Hecker and Rafi Segal designed it. Visitors move underground through a sequence of multimedia rooms, beginning with a memorial to the fallen. The plan zigzags at sharp angles around trees that were kept on the site, and the walls are faced with a local sandstone found while digging for the project. The design was shown at the Venice Biennale.

Museo Jumex, the main home of the Fundación Jumex Arte Contemporáneo and its collection, opened in November 2013 in the Polanco district of Mexico City, in a building by David Chipperfield. Zoning rules limited the space available, so Chipperfield moved the offices, shop and library into existing buildings next door and gave the museum itself almost entirely to exhibitions. The concrete structure stands on fourteen columns and is faced with travertine slabs from Xalapa in Veracruz, part of a design that responds to its setting and uses materials sourced in Mexico. Skylights on the roof, facing west, bring daylight into the upper galleries, while the lower floors have full-height windows framed in stainless steel. It belongs to the Plaza Carso mixed-use development, which includes a shopping mall, and faces the Museo Soumaya across the street.

Palacio Barolo is an office building at 1370 Avenida de Mayo, in the Monserrat district of Buenos Aires. Luis Barolo, an Italian immigrant who made his fortune in knitted fabrics, hired the Italian architect Mario Palanti to design it. Palanti admired Dante and shaped the building around the cosmology of the Divine Comedy. Its 22 floors fall into three parts: the basement and ground floor stand for hell, floors 1 to 14 for purgatory and 15 to 22 for heaven. It rises 100 metres, one for each canto, and nine vaulted arches spread from a central dome, standing for the nine circles of hell. On completion in 1923 no building in South America was taller, and it led the city until the Kavanagh Building of 1936. Its rooftop lighthouse was meant to welcome arrivals to the Río de la Plata.

The Rockefeller Archaeological Museum stands beside Herod's Gate in Jerusalem and holds a large collection of finds from digs in British-ruled Mandatory Palestine, mostly from the 1920s and 1930s. John D. Rockefeller Jr., the American philanthropist, agreed to give two million dollars towards it. Its architect, Austen Harrison, chief architect of the Mandate's Public Works Department, drew a white limestone building that blends eastern and western elements. Its foundation stone went down in June 1930, and it opened in January 1938, known as the Palestine Archaeological Museum until 1967. Over the entrance the British sculptor Eric Gill carved Asia meeting Africa; he also made ten reliefs of different cultures, a gargoyle fountain for the inner courtyard and stone signs in English, Hebrew and Arabic. The Dead Sea Scrolls were kept here from 1947 until 1967.

Yad Kennedy, a memorial to Kennedy, was paid for by American Jewish communities and built in 1966. It crowns the tallest of the Jerusalem hills, 825 metres high and 11 km from the city centre. David Resnick, an Israeli architect born in Brazil who later won the Israel Prize for architecture in 1995, designed it with Dov Feigin, an Israeli sculptor born in Ukraine. Because money came from groups in every state and in Washington, D.C., the idea of a column for each helped lead to the image of a tree trunk, a life felled in its prime. The 18-metre memorial is shaped like a cut stump, ringed by 51 concrete columns bearing state emblems and that of the capital, with slim glass strips between. Inside are a bronze relief of Kennedy and an eternal flame burning at the centre.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium, known as SVP Stadium, is in Ahmedabad's Navrangpura district, and India's first One Day International was played there. Sheth Chinubhai Chimanbhai, an industrialist then serving as mayor, hired Charles Correa to design the stadium and clubhouse, with Mahendra Raj as consulting structural engineer. Work began in 1959, but money ran short, and by 1966 only the roofed south pavilion was done; stands round the whole ground followed by the 1980s. It was the first building in India with a folded plate structure. The reinforced concrete cantilever roof over the pavilion, 20 metres wide and 326 feet long, was the world's longest span of its kind in 1963. Outside, geometric concrete frames leave open space under the seats. In 2020 the Getty Foundation gave it a grant, naming it among 13 significant twentieth-century buildings worldwide.

The Pakistan Monument on the western Shakarparian Hills in Islamabad serves as both national monument and heritage museum. It expresses the unity of the nation's people and honours those who sacrificed their own 'today' so that 'tomorrow' would be better. Arif Masoud's design was chosen from 21 entries and given approval on 10 July 2003. Its foundation stone went down on 25 May 2004, and President Pervez Musharraf opened it on 23 March 2007. The petals come from the muqarnas of Mughal architecture: four large granite petals stand for the Punjabi, Baloch, Sindhi and Pakhtun cultures, and three smaller ones for Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Kashmir and the minorities. They project as cantilevers, among Asia's largest. From the air the plan reads as the star and crescent of the national flag, and workers' handprints line the walls of Freedom Plaza.

Independence Memorial Hall stands in Independence Square in Colombo's Cinnamon Gardens. This national monument marks Sri Lanka's independence from British rule, when full governing power passed to an elected Ceylonese legislature on 4 February 1948, and occupies the spot where Prince Henry, Duke of Gloucester, opened the first parliament that day. Its design came from eight architects under Tom Neville Wynne-Jones, including Shirley de Alwis, Justin Samarasekera and F. H. Billimoria. The form follows the Magul Maduwa, royal audience hall of the Kingdom of Kandy, which was the island's last native kingdom. Until parliament moved to a new complex, it was the ceremonial assembly hall of the Senate and the House of Representatives; it now hosts religious events and the yearly national day. A statue of Don Stephen Senanayake, the first prime minister, stands at its head.

SOTA, the School of the Arts, is an independent specialist school in Singapore whose six-year course mixes arts training with academic study and ends in an International Baccalaureate diploma or a career-related programme. The 5.3-hectare campus sits at the foot of Mount Sophia in Bras Basah, its address 1 Zubir Said Drive. Credited to WOHA, the permanent campus cost S$145 million and was finished in 2009, and the school took up residence on 4 January 2010. At the 2010 World Architecture Festival it won the World Learning Building of the Year award, and in 2011 it received a RIBA International Award.

People's Park Complex is a tower of shops and flats on Park Road in Singapore's Outram area, beside Chinatown MRT station. Design Partnership, which William Lim co-founded in 1967, won the commission in its first year. At 31 storeys and 103 metres, it was Southeast Asia's first shopping centre of its type and a model for later retail in Singapore. The shopping centre was finished in October 1970 and the flats in 1973. The housing block has been called the nearest thing to the high-rise living Le Corbusier set out in his Marseille Unité d'Habitation; its 25 levels, nicknamed 'streets in the air', were meant for neighbours to meet. The mall holds Singapore's first 'city room', an idea of Japanese Metabolist architects: two interlocking multi-storey atriums holding many shops and kiosks. Its original finish was raw exposed concrete.

The Singapore Conference Hall is a five-storey modernist building by Lim Chong Keat, William Lim and Chan Voon Fee of Malayan Architects Co-Partnership, whose entry won a government competition in 1962. Finished in October 1965, it hosted conferences and exhibitions and housed the head office of the National Trades Union Congress. Concrete columns carry the cantilevered V-shaped roof and terraces, and the roof collects rain and drains it through a central downpipe. Although air-conditioned, the building also has natural ventilation worked into the design for the tropical climate. Walls and ceilings inside use local timbers such as merbau and mersawa to express local identity, and mosaic tiles in Malay mat patterns cover the walls. It houses the Singapore Chinese Orchestra in an 831-seat concert hall. No post-colonial building in Singapore had been gazetted as a national monument before it.

The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum is a large building at the centre of Ba Đình Square in Hanoi, where on 2 September 1945 Ho read out the Declaration of Independence. Building began on 2 September 1973 and the mausoleum was opened on 29 August 1975. The design is credited to Garol Isakovich. It draws on Lenin's Mausoleum in Moscow but adds Vietnamese features like its sloping roof. Grey granite clads the outside, while the inside uses polished grey, black and red stone. The structure measures 21.6 metres high and 41.2 metres wide, with two seven-step viewing platforms for parades. Ho's embalmed body rests in a dimly lit glass case in the cool central hall, under a military guard of honour. Nearly 250 species of plants and flowers from all over Vietnam grow in the gardens around it.

The Voortrekker Monument, a granite structure on a Pretoria hilltop, honours the Voortrekkers, who left the Cape Colony in 1835–1854. Gerard Moerdijk designed it, and Prime Minister D. F. Malan inaugurated it on 16 December 1949. Standing 62 metres high on a 40 by 40 metre base, it recalls European monuments such as the Dôme des Invalides and the Völkerschlachtdenkmal yet shows African influences. A gate leads into a laager of 64 granite ox-wagons, as many as at the Battle of Blood River. A vast inner space flanked by four arched windows of yellow Belgian glass holds the Historical Frieze, the world's biggest in marble. A round opening in the Hall of Heroes floor looks down on the Cenotaph; at noon each 16 December, sunlight through an oculus in the dome falls on its words 'Ons vir Jou, Suid-Afrika'.

Nasr City in Cairo is home to the Unknown Soldier Memorial, a monument in the shape of a pyramid. President Anwar Sadat ordered it in 1974 in honour of the Egyptians and Arabs who died in the October War of 1973, and it opened in October 1975. Its designer was Sami Rafi, an artist who taught at Cairo's Faculty of Fine Arts. The concrete form is a hollow pyramid, 25 metres high on a base 14.3 metres wide. Four pillars, 1.9 metres thick, bear 71 symbolic names, and in the middle of the base a solid basalt cube represents the soldier's tomb. When Sadat was assassinated in October 1981, the same site was chosen for his own grave.

MUAC, the Museo Universitario Arte Contemporáneo, is a large art museum on UNAM's main campus in Mexico City. It opened in November 2008 as Mexico's first public museum given over entirely to art of the 21st century. The architect, Teodoro González de León, also designed the COLMEX building and the Museo Rufino Tamayo, and worked with Abraham Zabludovsky on the National Auditorium. The museum belongs to the University Cultural Center, a vast group of auditoriums, galleries, libraries and research spaces. Its plain, sloping glass front stands apart from its neighbours, which were mostly designed in the 1970s, and its large, high-ceilinged halls can show many kinds of art. On the plaza in front rises La espiga, a carbon-steel sculpture by Rufino Tamayo more than 18 metres tall.
